text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

India: A Digital Dictatorship 

In recent years, India has earned an unfortunate title – the 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐡𝐮𝐭𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝. 
While the #internet has become an integral part of our Daily Lives, Enabling Communication, Commerce, and Information Access, India's frequent and prolonged #internet shutdowns have raised concerns about #Freedom, #Democracy, and Development in the World's Largest #Democracy.

The Alarming Rise in Internet Shutdowns

India's internet shutdowns have seen a disturbing rise in numbers, garnering international attention. 
These shutdowns are typically implemented by State Governments or authorities for various reasons, such as maintaining Law and Order, Curbing Protests, Preventing the Spread of Misinformation, and even during Critical Examinations to prevent cheating.

Key Statistics:

1. India has witnessed over 900 documented internet shutdowns from 2012 to 2021, according to the Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC).

2. In 2020, India alone accounted for nearly 67% of all documented internet shutdowns worldwide.

3. Some states, like Jammu and Kashmir, have experienced particularly prolonged and frequent shutdowns. (Now #Manipur)

The Impact on Democracy and Human Rights

Suppression of Freedom of Expression:
Internet shutdowns undermine the fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression. They curtail the ability of citizens to voice their opinions, access information, and engage in democratic discourse.

Economic Consequences: 
Shutdowns have severe economic implications. Small businesses, freelancers, and the digital economy suffer losses when access to the internet is denied.

Education Disruptions: 
Students' access to online education and educational resources is disrupted during shutdowns, exacerbating educational inequalities.

Healthcare Challenges: 
Access to telemedicine and health-related information becomes limited during internet shutdowns, affecting healthcare delivery.

The Legal Framework

India does have a legal framework governing the use of internet shutdowns. 
The primary legal basis for these shutdowns is Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), which empowers local authorities to impose restrictions on gatherings to maintain public order. However, its application to the digital sphere is contentious.

International Condemnation

India's internet shutdowns have faced International Condemnation and scrutiny. 
Human rights organizations and tech companies have raised concerns about the impact on democratic rights, and the #UnitedNations has stated that internet shutdowns should be a measure of last resort.

India's status as the Internet Shutdown Capital of the World is a cause for concern. 
While the government has cited security and public order reasons for these shutdowns, the scale and frequency of such measures raise questions about their proportionality and necessity.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

On 11 November 2026, my grievance was closed with a generic response explaining the IT Rules, 2021 and advising me to approach Facebook's Grievance Officer.

Were my previous complaints and supporting evidence reviewed?

Why was my explicit request for independent, higher-level intervention not addressed?

I have now formally escalated the matter to the Nodal Officer through CPGRAMS.

I am not seeking preferential treatment. I am seeking transparency, accountability and an impartial examination of my grievance.

A grievance redressal mechanism must deliver more than registration numbers and disposal remarks. It must deliver meaningful justice.

I respectfully request the intervention of the concerned authorities and an independent review by an appropriate senior authority.

If a citizen follows every prescribed procedure and still cannot obtain a meaningful response, where is that citizen supposed to go next?

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly objects to the takedown requests targeting its X handle and posts documenting instances of online censorship in India. 
 
On 3 November 2026 at 3:18 AM and 4:33 AM, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 received an email from X’s Legal Department informing us that it had received takedown requests from the Delhi Police concerning 42 URLs. These include the handles of https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, @internetfreedom, @geoblockedindia, and posts from the said organisations and other users. A separate notification identified five (5) URLs concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X account and our posts.

The requests relate to posts discussing legal notices received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). They also include posts by users who commented on or reshared these posts, as well as other posts by @geoblockedindia documenting instances of digital censorship.

Chain of Events

1. On 29 October 2026, when https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia (collectively “Organisations”) received a legal notice from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the RSS. The notice took objection to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's Free Speech Tracker, which documents instances of censorship and online content restrictions and account takedowns in India. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and IFF raised concerns about the authenticity of the notice, which did not carry an official letterhead or identify an authorised signatory.

2. On 1 November 2026, the Organisations received another notice from the same advocate. This notice stated that the matter had been transferred to the RSS's legal and advocacy wing, the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, and referred to complaints allegedly filed in different states.

3. On the same day, X informed https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 that it had received a request from the “Indian Police” alleging that a post discussing the legal notice violated Indian law. However, this notification did not identify the requesting law enforcement agency, statutory provisions invoked, or provide a copy of the underlying order or request. The post remains accessible on X at the time of writing.

4. On 3 November 2026, X communicated further directions from Delhi Police covering 42 URLs, including the URL for https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s account itself. In the attached notices, the first notice refers to Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 which deals with the offence of criminal defamation as the legal basis. The second notice refers to Section 356 of BNS and Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, read with Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology Rules 2021, which deal with intermediary liability and due diligence of intermediaries as the legal basis. The grounds cited for the takedown requests concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X handle and posts include hate speech, defamation of RSS, and safety/security.

Takedown requests targeting https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's handle threaten its public service work

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's X handle is an important public-facing channel through which it disseminates the organisation's ongoing work to the general public. It is through https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 social media handles that users who face digital rights violation and online harms reach out to us for pro bono legal services. Through the handle we publish legal and policy analysis, document instances of censorship, raise awareness about digital rights violations, and communicate such information with the public including journalists, researchers, civil society organisations among others. It also serves as a channel for sharing developments concerning internet shutdowns, content restrictions, account takedowns and other violations of digital rights and for providing important assistance, through RightsLine, to citizens facing online harms ranging from gender based violence and harassment  to cyberfraud. 

A direction seeking the takedown of an organisation’s entire account, rather than addressing specific content through a transparent and legally established process, would have consequences far beyond the posts that have been identified. It would also deprive the public of an established and credible source of information on digital rights and the exercise of fundamental freedoms online.

The request to restrict https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s entire X handle, rather than identifying and seeking the removal of specific allegedly unlawful content does not meet the necessity and proportionality standards. The right to freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution extends to disseminate information, circulate ideas and reach an audience.  Restrictions on fundamental freedoms must not be arbitrary or excessive and must not go beyond what is necessary to achieve their legitimate objective (Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1951 SC 118). Any restriction on an organisation's established channel of communication must therefore be assessed in light of its wider impact on the organisation's ability to exercise its rights and the public's corresponding right to receive information.

Further, the reliance on Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, raises questions to whether intermediary liability provisions are being used as an independent mechanism for restricting online speech, potentially bypassing the procedural safeguards prescribed under Section 69A of the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b), clarifying that an intermediary's obligation to remove or disable access to content must arise from a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency, and that such orders or notifications must strictly conform to the grounds enumerated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Section 79(3)(b), which forms part of the intermediary safe-harbour framework, cannot be treated as an unrestricted or independent source of blocking power or used to circumvent the safeguards governing restrictions on online information.

It is also pertinent to note that https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors, W.P.(C) 7650/2025 has also challenged the constitutional legality of the notification issued by Lieutenant Governor (LG) which empowers the Delhi Police to issue takedown orders for removal of online content from social media. The matter is currently pending in the Delhi High Court.

Documenting censorship is not facilitating circumvention

The Free Speech Tracker is an initiative to document instances of censorship in India. Its purpose is to make censorship visible, identify patterns in content moderation and provide the public with information about restrictions affecting online expression.

Documenting a restriction does not amount to endorsing the restricted content, facilitating access to it or encouraging circumvention of the law. Over the last few months, we have seen an unprecedented number of online content restrictions happening in India, and in the absence of adequate transparency from the government and platforms about the nature, extent and legal basis of these restrictions, we wanted to document these instances in a manner that is informative to the general public. Freedom of expression encompasses not only the right to publish and disseminate information but also the right to question restrictions on speech, seek accountability and scrutinise decisions affecting public discourse.

Independent civil society organisations like ours play an important role in documenting these developments and ensuring that restrictions on online expression do not go unnoticed. Such takedown requests risk creating a chilling effect on public-interest advocacy and may discourage individuals from discussing or questioning instances of censorship.

Irregularities in notice received

The first notice received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 from X, pertains to this post. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of ‘safety/security; defamation; and other’. Furthermore, the notice states that the post is “defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under the Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).” Criminal defamation under Section 356 of the BNS, 2023, is a non-cognizable offence and therefore, requires a court order for the police to initiate action.

The second notice received, pertains to a list of 42 posts and accounts. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of “Hate speech; safety/security; defamation; enforcement of court order; and other’. The posts published by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 did not contain any defamatory statements or allegations against RSS, as it was purely factual reporting based on information relating to the notice received by the Organisations on 29 October 2026.

Furthermore, criminal defamation is a non-cognizable offence which requires a court order for the police to initiate action. The Delhi Police is not empowered to issue a content takedown order for such offence via the Sahyog Portal in the absence of such an order. While the notice mentions enforcement of a court order as one of the grounds, no such court order is cited or made available in the notice. Additionally, the notice does not identify a legal basis or statutory provision for the offences of hate speech or safety/security. The notice also relies on Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and states that action must be taken by X within 3 hours.

Therefore, in light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 condemns the takedown request issued by the Delhi Police and maintains that they are unlawful, disproportionate and violative of the fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police and the concerned authorities to immediately withdraw these requests. If there exists any relevant court order directing the removal of the content, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police to provide copies of said order to the Organisations (https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF, and @geoblockedindia) posthaste. 

We stand in solidarity with all individuals and organisations affected by these takedown requests and reaffirm our commitment to defending their right to speak, document and question restrictions on online expression. Transparency, accountability and access to remedies must remain central to any process that seeks to restrict online expression.

Supreme Court stays GST demands on corporate guarantees: what the interim order does, and what it leaves untouched

The Supreme Court has stayed the GST demands raised on corporate guarantees given within groups, pending a challenge to the Gujarat High Court's August 2026 ruling on Rule 28(2) of the CGST Rules. The stay is interim. It does not decide taxability and it does not strike down the rule.

For groups sitting on show cause notices or adjudication orders on guarantees given to banks for subsidiaries, this buys time. It does not buy certainty.

Background

Rule 28(2) was inserted by Notification 52/2023-Central Tax with effect from 26 October 2023. It values a corporate guarantee given to a related person at 1% per annum of the amount guaranteed, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher. Circular 204/16/2023-GST of 27 October 2023 explained the rule, and Circular 225/19/2024-GST of 11 July 2024 answered a list of trade questions. Notification 12/2024-Central Tax then amended the rule retrospectively from 26 October 2023 to extend the benefit of the second proviso to Rule 28(1): where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the invoice value is deemed to be the value of supply.

Circular 225 also settled the mechanics. Guarantees issued or renewed before 26 October 2023 are valued under the old Rule 28; those issued or renewed on or after that date fall under Rule 28(2). Value is based on the amount guaranteed, not the amount disbursed. A multi-year guarantee is taxed at issuance at 1% for each year of its term, pro-rated for part years, and each renewal is a fresh supply. Co-guarantors share the value in proportion to the amount each guarantees. A foreign related party guaranteeing an Indian entity's borrowing triggers reverse charge in India, and Rule 28(2) does not apply where the recipient is outside India.

The Gujarat High Court ruling

On 14 August 2026, a Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court partly allowed a batch of petitions. It upheld Rule 28(2) and section 15(4) of the CGST Act, and accepted that a guarantee given to a related person without consideration is a taxable supply. It read down the words "whichever is higher" as arbitrary, because they deny the guarantor the option of using the actual charge. In the matters before it, actual charges ranged between 0.25% and 0.3%, well below the 1% deemed value.

The High Court also held the 1% valuation harsh for guarantees given before 26 October 2023, while keeping liability from that date. It quashed section 74 proceedings where there was no deliberate suppression; one notice of August 2024 related to a guarantee of February 2012. It directed refund of excess GST, set aside the conflicting circular clarifications and allowed three months for implementation.

What the Supreme Court has done

Petitions against that judgment came up on 16 November 2026 before a Bench of Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice Vipul M. Pancholi. The Court issued notice, returnable in four weeks, and stayed the impugned demands until further orders. The order records no findings on merits.

Read it narrowly. The demands in the matters before the Court are stayed. Rule 28(2) stands. The Gujarat reading-down stands as one High Court's view, now under challenge. Officers elsewhere may continue to issue notices, and other High Courts are not bound by the Gujarat ruling.

Who is affected

Indian holding companies that guarantee bank loans of subsidiaries, step-down entities and joint ventures. Promoter-group entities that cross-guarantee each other's working capital limits. Indian subsidiaries of foreign groups where the parent guarantees local borrowings, since they pay under reverse charge. Lenders and statutory auditors who need to know whether the guarantor's books carry a contingent GST exposure.

The practitioner's view

The real money in these disputes is rarely the tax on fully creditable transactions. Where the borrowing subsidiary is a regular taxpayer entitled to full ITC, the second proviso to Rule 28(1) lets the invoice value stand, and whatever the parent pays comes back to the group as credit. The exposure sits in three places: recipients making exempt supplies or otherwise not eligible for full credit, pre-October 2023 periods where notices have applied the 1% yardstick, and section 74 notices that use the extended period to reach back several years.

The stay helps the petitioners directly. For everyone else it signals that the Supreme Court sees a serious question. That is a reason to defend notices on merits and limitation, not a reason to ignore them. An order left unappealed within time becomes final, whatever the Supreme Court later decides.

The second issue is records. Many groups do not keep a register of guarantees with amount, tenure, renewal dates and the borrower's ITC position. Without it, exposure cannot be computed under either reading of the rule.

Take an illustration on the circular's method. A parent guarantees a ₹100 crore term loan of its subsidiary for five years. Value is 5% of ₹100 crore, that is ₹5 crore, taxed at issuance at 18%, giving ₹90 lakh. If the subsidiary is entitled to full ITC, the invoice value can be accepted under the second proviso and the tax is a timing cost. If the subsidiary's outward supplies are partly exempt, that relief is not available and part of the ₹90 lakh becomes a real cost. Under the Gujarat reading, an actual charge of 0.3% a year would give a value of ₹1.5 crore instead.

Action points

1. Build a guarantee register for every guarantee issued or renewed since July 2017: beneficiary, lender, amount, term, renewals, fee charged and the borrower's ITC eligibility.

2. Split the exposure into periods before and after 26 October 2023, since the valuation rule and the litigation position differ.

3. Where a notice invokes section 74, test it for actual suppression. Disclosure in audited financial statements and in the borrower's records weakens any allegation of intent.

4. File replies and appeals within time, and ask that proceedings be kept in abeyance by citing the pending Supreme Court matter. Do not let an order become final by default.

5. For new guarantees, document the fee on arm's length lines and the borrower's eligibility for full ITC, so the second proviso to Rule 28(1) can be applied cleanly.

6. Where the guarantor is abroad, confirm that the Indian borrower is paying under reverse charge and taking the matching credit.

7. Brief the statutory auditor on the contingent liability and the basis for any provision or disclosure.

The stay gives four weeks of breathing room and, in practice, probably far more. Use it to put the facts in order, because when the Court rules, the group with clean records will be better placed whichever way it goes.

This is general information, not advice on any specific case.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

The Kerala High Court on Tuesday (28 April) issued notice on a plea filed by Madhyamam Broadcasting Limited, broadcaster of Media One news channel, challenging blocking of its official Facebook page in India.

Justice K.V. Jayakumar issued the notice to the respondents and directed the Central government and Meta to file counter affidavits.

The petitioner, contends that its Facebook page was abruptly rendered “not available in India” on April 23, 2026, following a notification citing a request from the Government of India or law enforcement under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

According to the petition, the blocking has effectively cut off access to MediaOne's digital content for Indian users, disrupting its online operations and causing significant financial loss.

The broadcaster states that its Facebook page, active since 2011, is a key platform for disseminating news and public interest content and generates substantial revenue estimated at around ₹25 lakh per month.

The petitioner alleges that the action was taken without disclosure of any blocking order under Section 69A of the IT Act, communication of reasons or prior notice or opportunity of hearing.

The petitioner argues that the actions of the respondents is a complete disregard of the mandatory statutory safeguards and constitutional limitations governing online content regulation.

The Petitioner further submitted that the Section 79(3)(b) invoked in the notification, does not confer independent powers to block content. Instead, it only outlines circumstances in which intermediaries lose safe harbour protection.

The petitioner relies on the Supreme Court's ruling in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India [(2015) 5 SCC 1], which held that “actual knowledge” for content takedown must arise only through a court order or a valid government blocking order under Section 69A.

The petition contends that no such court order or Section 69A direction has been disclosed and argues that intermediaries cannot act on informal or undisclosed executive communications.

The petitioner has also challenged the scope of the restriction, arguing that the law permits blocking only of “specific and identifiable content,” not entire accounts or pages.

The blanket disabling of its Facebook page, it claims, is excessive, disproportionate, and contrary to the statutory framework under the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009.

Further, the petition points to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which require that blocking directions be content-specific and not result in cessation of operations.

It is further submitted that the blocking violates the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 19(1)(g), as well as its property rights under Article 300A of the Constitution of India.

The petitioner has thus sought to set aside the blocking of its Facebook page, declare the action illegal and unconstitutional, direct restoration of access within India, and ensure compliance with statutory safeguards for any future content regulation.

The Court has issued the notice to the respondents and has posted the matter to 5 MAy for further consideration.

Prominent Malayalam news channel MediaOne TV has approached the Kerala High Court challenging the blocking of its Facebook page, alleging that the action was arbitrary and in violation of Supreme Court rulings as well as the Information Technology Act.

The petition states that the Facebook page “MediaOne TV” was restricted on Friday, with access blocked specifically for users in India. The channel argued that the page was blocked without citing any specific content or violation.

Following this, the channel moved the High Court seeking relief against the action.

Despite the restriction in India, the page remains accessible outside the country, and administrative functions such as uploading news and videos have not been affected.

Earlier, in January 2022, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting barred MediaOne TV from broadcasting, citing “national security reasons” and denial of security clearance by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

However, in April 2023, the Supreme Court of India quashed the ban, observing that national security claims cannot be made “out of thin air” without material evidence, and that criticism of government policies does not render a channel “anti-national.”

Fake court orders how? Why? Top 10.

As per Reuters, DoT got 129 websites blocked on two fake High Court orders. Last week X told the Delhi HC that the Delhi Police orders against IFF were fake too.

1. Too many censorship bodies. MeitY, MHA, MIB, DoT, state governments, police and courts all issue takedown or blocking orders.

2. Too many censorship laws. 69A, 79(3)(b), IT Rules, BNSS notices, court orders, each with its own format, so nobody knows what a real order should look like. The Sahyog platform by templatisation has only automated the process, not made the orders intelligible. 

3. Pressure on platforms to act immediately, even pre-censor. The deadline is three hours and nobody can verify an order in that time.

4. No one to check, just censor. DoT got a fake High Court order on email on a Sunday night and told ISPs to block 34 sites two days later. It was not even on the court's website. Our government is incompetent and trigger happy to take down even global web services. Full domain and app blocking is now a norm. 

5. Notices have no legal threshold and rely on subjective perception of offence and vibez. A fake one reads the same as a real one. What’s fact or fiction when our censorship regime is based on magic realism. 

6. MeitY is incompetent and can only pressure Silicon Valley platforms to take down more and faster. Ask who issued an order and it says not us. It does not want to provide statistics, shies away from transparency and every six months gets the itch to amend the IT Rules, 2021. 

7. Courts pass John Doe and dynamic injunctions so often that lawyers emailing DoT a new list of sites to block is normal. One more email from an "advocate" is not sus to anyone.

8. Orders are kept secret. The person censored rarely gets a copy so they can't say it is fake. We found out only because X forwarded the notices to us, and Reuters because DoT puts court orders online (this category is a rare exception). 

9. Platforms are punished only for not complying. Ignore a real order and you lose safe harbour and staff can be prosecuted. Obey a fake one and nothing happens lol.

10. Much of this is automated. Meta reportedly acts on government flags without human review and I4C says it has no record of notices sent through Sahyog.

Quite simply, censorship is the norm and speech is put to suspicion.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

First, under Section 69A, which allows the government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. Read with Rule 16 of the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009, this provision requires confidentiality regarding all requests and complaints received, as well as actions taken.

Second, Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

# Bangladesh Home Minister and UN Special Rapporteur Discuss Repatriation of Bengali Refugees

AK- News English/November 13, 2026

Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed and Kelley E. Currie, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, held talks on November 12, 2026, at the Home Ministry office inside the Bangladesh Secretariat in Dhaka, with the repatriation of Bengali refugees emerging as a key topic of discussion.

According to reports, the meeting focused on Myanmar’s current political and human rights situation, the safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of Bengalis sheltering in Bangladesh, border security, and law and order conditions in refugee camps.

During the meeting, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said that although official documents recorded a lower figure, more than 1.5 million Bengalis were actually living in Bangladesh. He described hosting such a large population over an extended period as a significant economic burden on the country.

He stressed that the ultimate goal of international efforts should be to ensure the safe, voluntary and dignified return of Bengalis to their homeland, Myanmar. He also called on the international community to engage responsibly following the International Court of Justice (ICJ)'s scheduled November 19, 2026, ruling in the case concerning genocide against Bengalis in Myanmar.

UN Special Rapporteur Kelley E. Currie praised the Bangladesh government for providing long-term humanitarian shelter and assistance to Bengali refugees. Referring to historical human rights violations committed against the Bengali population, she explained that the United Nations and its international partners were working to create conditions conducive to repatriation and to ensure that citizenship rights and fundamental freedoms would be guaranteed in their homeland.

The two sides also held constructive discussions on strengthening the capacity of law enforcement agencies to combat drug trafficking, arms smuggling and cybercrime in and around refugee camps. The discussions included the provision of necessary training and modern technological assistance.

In addition, the meeting highlighted the importance of coordinated diplomatic pressure on the Myanmar government by influential international actors, including China, India, the United States and the European Union.

Also attending the meeting were Thomas Hunecke, the Special Rapporteur's mission focal point; Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed, Deputy Secretary of the Political and Immigration Wing of Bangladesh's Ministry of Home Affairs; and Rebecca Khan, Joint Secretary of the Political-1 Division.
