INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

A lot of people need to understand the difference between the metric system and the imperial system before ordering from shopping platforms like Temu.

Most sellers list product measurements using the metric system, so you’ll often see sizes in centimetres (cm) rather than inches. For example, 10 cm is NOT 10 inches. In fact, 10 cm is only about 3.94 inches.

So if you’re used to thinking in inches, don’t just look at “10 cm” and assume it’s 10 inches. Convert the measurement first so you know exactly what you’re buying.

For reference:
• 1 inch = 2.54 cm
• 10 cm ≈ 3.94 inches
• 20 cm ≈ 7.87 inches
• 30 cm ≈ 11.81 inches
• 50 cm ≈ 19.69 inches

Please read the product specifications and measurements before adding anything to your cart. Check the dimensions, convert them into the unit you understand, and compare them with something you already have at home if necessary.

I personally do believe in karma and think the Russini return is having some type of impact, or just that situation in general has had an impact on his ability to be a leader of men. I mean he did cheat on his wife, lie about it, skipped out on the NFL Draft, then he was caught on video drinking beer with fans the night before this game. Accountability matters in the NFL, especially as a head coach. It looks like Maye will miss considerable time, and Tommy DeVito was truly horrible in relief. Things are going to get a lot worse for the Patriots before they get better. The win for Detroit masked a horrible self-inflicted wound with star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson tearing his own ACL while celebrating the sack which also knocked Maye out of the game. Karma is truly undefeated. No upgrade for Detroit because whatever they gained from this performance they lost with the Hutchinson injury. Obviously a significant downgrade for New England going from Maye to DeVito. I make that at least a 7-point move.

Chiefs 35, Falcons 13
Kansas City won the box score (+1.7 net YPP, +11.1% net SR) and won turnovers (2-0). Patrick Mahomes had his best EPA performance since Week 13 last season despite no Kenneth Walker. Emmet Johnson (22 car, 101 rush yds, 6 rec, 70 rec yds, 2 rec TD) continues to be a revelation and Josh Downs (4 rec, 53 rec yds, 1 rec TD) looked good in his KC debut. The Falcons struggled in the high-leverage moments and went just 1-for-5 scoring TDs in the RZ. George Karlaftis had 7 pressures and has the 2nd most pressures in the NFL this season. Kansas City is a very balanced team (7th EPA per play on offense, 5th on defense) and will be a very tough out in January especially if they win the division and get to play at home. Oh by the way Mahomes was doing all of this with an injured elbow that required him to see a specialist with the Kansas City Royals this week who specializes in UCL tears. He is truly a cyborg. I think it’s fair to say the Michael Penix Jr. experiment is over and Atlanta wasted a first round pick on him two years ago. To make matters worse Kirk Cousins looks fully healthy and thriving with the Vikings, which is the QB they signed weeks before drafting Penix before letting him walk this past offseason. Total disaster move that has set the franchise back years. Slight upgrade for Kansas City. Slightly bigger downgrade Atlanta.

Browns 27, Texans 24
Cleveland won the box score (+1.2 net YPP, +7.5% net SR) turnovers were even (1-1) and Houston won sacks (4-1) but got lost penalties (-65 net yards) in a very disjointed performance. The Texans quickly jumped out to a 17-0 lead but got outscored 27-7 the remainder of the game.  Houston is now 1-5 in one-score games this season so they are essentially the anti-Broncos. I think a lot of that falls on the shoulders of DeMeco Ryans but also the fact that they can’t run the ball a lick makes it harder to win close games. They need a certain type of game script in order to be successful and it’s just hard to win that way week after week in the NFL when you consistently have to put the ball in the air to sustain offense down to down. Meanwhile Cleveland has been very impressive in close games this season and has already exceeded their win total of 5.5. Todd Monken deserves to be coach of the year. They’re 4-0 at home and have silenced a lot of doubters but I’m personally still not a believer in this team longterm. Except for their Thursday night win over the Steelers all of their wins have come against teams under .500 and I would even argue the win over Pittsburgh is not aging well. That being said, I still have to upgrade them this week for winning outright as a dog of more than 3 points. I also have to downgrade Houston significantly. I’ve been a defender of the Texans for weeks and have backed them several times but I’m starting to think I was completely wrong about this team, especially the defense, in being able to turn it around and make the playoffs.

Vikings 30, Packers 10
Minnesota won the box score (+0.8 net YPP, +8.3% net SR) and won turnovers (4-1). Jordan Love got sacked 8 times by this aggressive Vikings defense and the explosive Packers offense had one of their worst performances of the season in terms of EPA on early downs and dropbacks. This should have been an easy handicap on that side of the ball. The only way to beat the Vikings defense is to run it, and the Packers have the worst rushing offense in the NFL. On the other side you have to give Kirk Cousins all the flowers. He was handed the playbook about 72 hours before the game and operated the offense flawlessly on the road against a divisional opponent. The interview after the game got me choked up. I forgot that Lambeau Field is where he tore his Achilles in his last game with the Vikings three years ago. Karma is real. Justin Jeferson had a 43.3% target share, his highest since Week 5 of the 2024 season. The Vikings also produced their best EPA per dropback and EPA per designed rush of the season. Minnesota looks like a legit Super Bowl contender in a wide open NFC with Cousins at the helm and the best defense in the league. Green Bay is too one dimensional to be taken seriously. They remind me of the Texans. Zero run game, if they aren’t hitting explosives in the pass game they are very beatable. It also reminds me of a home run hitting team in baseball that doesn’t do the little things well or play station to station. That makes them a tough team to bet on most weeks, unless they are facing a defense like the Vikings that you know will keep the explosives in check. Major upgrade Minnesota. It’s fair to say they should be ranked just behind the top tier teams in the NFC like San Francisco and the Rams when at full strength. Slightly smaller downgrade Green Bay. They clearly have holes on their roster and desperately need Micah Parsons back.

Jaguars 40, Titans 23
Jacksonville won the box score (+0.8 net YPP, +13.5% net SR) turnovers and sacks were even. The difference in this game was the Jaguars controlled time of possession and wore out the Titans defense which eventually caved. Cam Ward had a few nice moments despite not having his top pass catcher Carnell Tate. I thought Tennessee played well enough to keep it within the number (Titans +10.5) but they couldn’t convert a 4th and 1 in the final minutes which allowed Jacksonville to score the final touchdown and front door the spread. We’ve learned now that Ward has recently taken over more control of the offense at the line of scrimmage, which I think is a positive for his development. If you zoom out from their 1-8 record the offense hasn’t been terrible the last four weeks scoring 26, 24, 36, and 23 points. The problem is they are still turning it over too much and the defense has not helped them out at all. Tennessee is 17th in EPA per play on offense this season and 29th on defense. Ward is ranked 20th out of 29 qualifiers in adjusted EPA per play. Definitely not bottom of the barrel type stuff. You would have expected the defense to be better and show improvement under Robert Saleh, but I guess that is asking too much, especially after they traded away their best safety (Amari Hooker) and best defensive lineman (Jeffrey Simmons) in the last two weeks. The Jags keep humming along and haven’t trailed in a game since their Week 6 loss to the Texans in London over a month ago. Parker Washington (9 rec, 152 rec yds, 1 rec TD) is one of the most underrated receivers in the NFL. Jacksonville has an incredibly easy schedule down the stretch so they are in strong contention for the No. 1 seed in the AFC. They are the most balanced team in the NFL (3rd in EPA per play on offense, 4th on defense) and Liam Coen is one of the best young coaches and playcallers in the sport. Their big trade deadline acquisitions (Jessie Bates, Jordan Davis) didn’t play in this game as the team wanted to give them their bye week, so expect the defense to get even better. Jacksonville needs to be taken very seriously as a legit Super Bowl contender. Slight upgrade Jags. Slight downgrade Titans.

Colts 24, Dolphins 22
Indianapolis won the box score, barely (+0.4 net YPP, +4.7% net SR) but lost turnovers (1-2) and penalties (-53 net yards). Miami actually had a slightly better PGWE (post-game win expectancy) so it’s fair to say they should have won this game. Daniel Jones posted a 1.7 QBR, the worst of any QB in a start this season. Even worse than the Carson Wentz MNF performance against the BIlls and Baker Mayfield’s zero-completion game. He looks awkward and disjointed every time he drops back to throw. I give credit to the Dolphins for battling in this game despite Kyle McCord making his first career start at QB. The only Miami player to throw a touchdown pass in the last two weeks is WR Malik Washington. They are showing fight but clearly lack any premier talent at key positions besides a decent pass rush with Chop Robinson causing havoc. I made the mistake of using the Colts in my spread pool this week and I am kicking myself for laying points with Daniel Jones. Never again. Despite winning this game I’m going to downgrade Indy for as long as they keep Jones as the starter. No downgrade for Miami who continue to show fight and are 4-5 ATS this season despite only winning one game outright.

Panthers 20, Saints 17
Carolina won YPP (4.4 to 3.6) but New Orleans won SR (34.4% to 32.3%). The Panthers won turnovers (2-0) and sacks were even. This game reminded me a lot of the Giants and Commanders game on Thursday. Two evenly matched teams in a bad division that came down to who had the ball last. Bryce Young played okay but he has been trending down since the breakout win over the Lions in Week 4. The Panthers are 2-3 since that game with their only wins over the Eagles without Jalen Hurts and yesterday by the skin of their teeth against the Saints. Young is also the 3rd most sacked QB (29) in the NFL this season. The biggest issue for Carolina is self-inflicted wounds. They lead the NFL in penalties per game (9.7) and penalty yards per game (87.2) by a wide margin. The Saints offense has fallen off a cliff despite the return of Jordyn Tyson. They are dead last in EPA per rush. They also rank dead last in first quarter and first half scoring. After throwing for 1,206 yards his first four games, Tyler Shough has only thrown for 970 in his last five. Slight upgrade Carolina for simply winning this shitfest. Slight downgrade New Orleans who seem to be trending in the wrong direction.

Bills 31, Jets 12
Buffalo won the box score (+2.2 net YPP, +3% net SR) and won turnovers (2-1). Geno Smith got knocked out of the game on a vicious hit that probably would have been flagged if it was Josh Allen or Patrick Mahomes on the other end of it. Geno tried to come back in the game but clearly he wasn’t feeling 100% right. Cade Klubnik was awful in relief. The Bills have now won three straight games where the majority of snaps were taken by backup and third string opposing quarterbacks (Joe Fagnano, Carson Wentz, Cade Klubnik). They will get another scenario like that this week against Kyle McCord and also play the Patriots in three weeks possibly without Drake Maye depending on the severity of his injury. Buffalo also plays the Jets and Dolphins the final two weeks of the season. To be fair, their other opponents (Chiefs, Packers, Bears, Broncos) will challenge them, but it’s hard to tell just how good the Bills are this season, especially on defense. Aaron Glenn said after the game he gave up defensive play-caller duties to DC Brian Duker. He didn’t call the defense last year but took back over the responsibilities this season calling it his “superpower.” I have no idea if it will help this Jets defense which is ranked 32nd in EPA per play since Week 6 which is when their current five-game losing streak began. I’m not upgrading Buffalo because they simply have not been challenged yet and I don’t want to overreact to their big margins the last three weeks. I will wait on Geno news before I adjust the Jets rating. I make Geno to Klubnik a 4-point downgrade but it might be closer to 6 after watching him play on Sunday.

Seahawks 21, Raiders 13
Seattle dominated the box score (+4.6 net YPP, +17.8% net SR) but lost turnovers (0-2). Fernando Mendoza looked good on the opening drive thanks to a strong Klint Kubiak script that used play action on every dropback. Mendoza finished 20th out of 27 qualifiers in EPA per dropback. Not horrible considering the defense he was facing, but not great either. The big problem for him right now is there is zero run game or threat of verticality from his receivers. His only real weapons are tight ends, and you can’t sustain offense like that in the NFL. You need to be able to threaten on the outside. On the flipside, Drew Lock had the 5th highest EPA per dropback number of the week which is impressive when you consider how many great quarterback performances and high-scoring games there were last week. He has filled in incredibly well for Sam Darnold and dare I say there is a quarterback controversy brewing in Seattle. I think Darnold deserves to get his job back once he is healthy, but if he struggles at any point I think his leash will be much shorter now.The Seahawks are in a similar situation to the Vikings, Mike Macdonald cannot waste a historically good defense on below-average quarterback play. The part about Lock’s play that has been incredibly impressive, zero interceptions in four games this season. Essentially the anti-Darnold. Slight upgrade for Seattle. Slight downgrade Vegas. When Darnold returns after the bye next week I will likely keep the Seahawks rating about the same.

Rams 34, Cardinals 6
Los Angeles dominated the box score (+2.5 net YPP, +24.8% net SR) and won turnovers (2-1). After the first quarter this game was pretty much belt to ass. Arizona ran just 34 plays which was the 2nd fewest for a team in a game this season. The Rams defense dominated and Carson Beck’s NFL debut went about as expected. He finished 27th out of 27 qualifiers in EPA per dropback. Anyone who doubted Sean McVay and Nathan Scheelhaase’s ability to call a good game without the Rams elite weapons on the outside clearly haven’t been paying attention much over the last few years. The biggest concern I have with this Rams team is the health of Matthew Stafford. I have faith Puka and DaVante will eventually return and this team will make the playoffs. The schedule is tough so they might not win the division but I also have faith they have the ability to go on the road and win playoff games in outdoor conditions. The defense is starting to mold themselves into one of the most dominant units in the sport, especially up front. That shouldn’t come as a surprise considering the personnel. It doesn’t get any easier for the Rams from here with the Packers, Chiefs, and 49ers on deck, but this also might be the cheapest price you get them at for the rest of the year if they find ways to go 2-1 or even 3-0 in that stretch. Meanwhile Arizona is devolving back into the lemon we thought they were going to be before the season started, which was a 2 or 3-win team. Beck will gain some valuable experience during this stretch but when your top weapons at receiver are Devin Duvernay and Simi Fehoko there is only so much you can do. Slight upgrade Rams. Slight downgrade Arizona.

49ers 46, Cowboys 40
San Francisco won the bos score (+1.7 net YPP, +1.6% net SR) and won turnovers (2-0). The only negative for the Niners in this game is Brock Purdy took 5 sacks and the team committed 11 penalties for 100 yards which were both season highs. Despite those hiccups, Purdy continues to lead the NFL in EPA per dropback. Dallas has the worst defense in the NFL (32nd in EPA per play allowed) and it isn’t particularly close. They rank 26th in passing yards per game allowed, 32nd in rushing yards allowed, 32nd in total yards allowed, and 30th in points allowed. They are the only team to allow at least 20 points in every game this season. I would imagine DC Christian Parker gets fired at some point before the end of the year but with Jerry Jones running the show who knows how it will play out. Dak Prescott attempted 51 passes, the most by far of any quarterback in Week 10. The irony is that they are actually an efficient running team (6th in EPA per rush) but the game script rarely allows it because of how poorly their defense plays. We will learn a lot more about how good the Niners offense really is this week when they face the best defense in the league (Vikings) in weird conditions at altitude in Mexico City. Slight upgrade San Francisco. Slight downgrade Dallas. I currently have the Niners as my highest power rated team in the NFL (+6.4) just ahead of Buffalo (+6.2).

Bengals 38, Steelers 18 (SNF)
Cincinnati dominated the box score (+3.8 net YPP, +17.3% net SR) turnovers were flat and the Bengals won sacks (3-1). This game felt non-competitive from the start. Pittsburgh looked completely flat off the bye. Joe Burrow had the 2nd highest EPA per dropback number of the week just behind Brock Purdy with 4 touchdowns and 409 yards passing. He is now the MVP favorite and rightfully so after slicing the league up the last five weeks since their loss to the Jaguars in Week 4. That loss is also aging very well. Cincinnati has scored at least 31 points in all five games during this win streak. They play the Commanders, Saints, and Browns the next three weeks so I don’t expect them to slow down. Pittsburgh gets a layup against the Eagles next week before things get a little tougher down the stretch with games against the Broncos, Texans, Jaguars, Ravens (twice) to close the season. If I had to make a bet right now on the Steelers to make or miss the playoffs I would bet miss which is currently being priced around +200 odds. Big upgrade Cincinnati. Slightly smaller downgrade Pittsburgh.

Chargers 23, Ravens 20 (MNF)
The box score was relatively even but the Chargers won turnovers (2-0) and played their cleanest game of the season winning their first game and getting off the proverbial schneid. Justin Herbert had handcuffs put on him by Mike McDaniel with a very conservative gameplan. Herbert finished with the 3rd fewest air yards among qualified QBs and attempted just 18 passes. The reason that was possible is the Chargers were in a positive game script for the first time all season and jumped out to a quick 10-0 lead before Jacoby Brissett could get settled in for the Ravens. I didn’t think Brissett played poorly, he finished about middle of the pack in EPA per dropback, the Ravens just couldn’t control the line of scrimmage with Derrick Henry running for 10 yards on 10 carries. Baltimore has now dropped 5 in a row and is in complete freefall after losing to the worst team in the league. I’m not sure where they go from here with the Panthers, Texans, and Bucs on deck the next three weeks before closing the season with four straight divisional games (Steelers x2, Browns, Bengals). I think Jim Harbaugh’s familiarity with Ravens HC Mike Minter’s defensive scheme was a factor in this game. Herbert’s legs were the most effective part of this game and he looked decisive for the first time all season. Slight upgrade Chargers, slightly bigger downgrade Ravens.

This severely weakens citizens right to access information, question authority, scrutinise decision-making, carry out public audits & demand accountability from those in power. Through the SIR exercise, it has become clear how critical access to granular personal information is - wrongful deletions of voters came to light and could be challenged only because the Supreme Court directed public disclosure of the list of deleted voters and those issued notices. 
• By failing to exempt journalists from its ambit, the DPDP Act, has become a death knell for press freedom.

text: Privacy vs Press Freedom: Where Should the Line Be Drawn? https://t.co/lMP2vkkXLu

🔸The Challenge to the DPDP Act
- Petitioner
DNPA (21 publishers); petition filed 6 October, stay sought 27 October.

- Concerns
Could expose sources, force removal of reports and deter whistleblowers.

- Consent problem
Seeking consent from subjects = 'pre-censorship' (Madhavi Divan).

- No exemption
The Act has no specific journalistic exemption.

🔸Relevant Provisions of the DPDP Act
- Section 3(c)(ii)
Excludes data made public by the person or under a legal duty – a limited exclusion.

- Sections 4–6
Grounds, notice and consent for processing personal data.

- Section 8
Duties of data fiduciaries – security, accuracy, erasure.

- Section 17
Exemptions for legal proceedings, law enforcement, research – not journalism.

🔸The Constitutional Balance
- Right to Privacy
Article 21 – dignity, autonomy, personal data (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

- Press freedom
Article 19(1)(a) – investigate and report on public interest.

- Limits
Both are not absolute; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.

🔸Key Judgments
- R. Rajagopal (1994)
'Auto Shankar case' – officials can't use privacy to block reports on official conduct; no prior restraint.

- R.K. Anand (2009)
Upheld a sting operation exposing an attempt to subvert the BMW trial.

- Manu Sharma (2010)
Warned against media trials that turn suspects into convicts.

- Sahara v. SEBI (2012)
Courts may postpone reporting if there is real risk to a fair trial.

- Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014)
Sting journalism gives no blanket immunity for unlawful acts.

- Axel Springer v. Germany (2012)
ECHR Grand Chamber (12–5) upheld a newspaper's report on an actor's arrest as public-interest journalism.

🔸Global Approaches
- USA
First Amendment; Privacy Protection Act, 1980 limits searches of journalists' work.

- UK
Data Protection Act, 2018 – exemption if publication is in the public interest.

- Brazil
General Data Protection Law excludes journalisticprocessing.

- Kenya
Section 52, Data Protection Act, 2019 – conditional exemption.

- International law
Articles 17 & 19 ICCPR; Articles 8 & 10 ECHR.

🔸Way Forward
- Journalistic exemption
A narrow, public-interest exemption in the DPDP framework.

- Public interest test
Separate genuine scrutiny from needless intrusion.

- Source protection
Protect sources while ensuring accuracy and fairness.

- Proportionality
Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate.

The Supreme Court hears the Digital News Publishers Association's challenge to the DPDP Act tomorrow, 17 November 2026.

The petition challenges sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37 and 44(3) of the Act and Rules 16, 17 and 23 of the DPDP Rules. Senior Advocate Madhavi Divan argued for DNPA on 27 October that the consent requirements could disrupt the work of newsrooms.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana issued notice on the petition and the stay application on 27 October. The court did not stay any provision.

Since then, the News Broadcasters & Digital Association has written to the IT Minister for a journalism exemption, and unnamed government sources told PTI on 7 November that journalists are not Data Fiduciaries. By my reading, none of this has changed the text of the Act.

Of the challenged provisions, sections 18, 19 and 44(3) and Rule 17 are already in force. Most of the others start on 13 May 2027.

Reported by MediaNews4U, 27 October 2026: https://t.co/laoC3VcSzU

Deep Concern over the Removal of Millions of Muslim Names from India's Revised Electoral Rolls

Bangladesh Islami Chhatrashibir has expressed deep concern over the removal of nearly 130 million names from India's nationwide electoral rolls through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, warning that the voting rights and citizenship security of a significant number of eligible Muslim voters could be jeopardised. Central President Nurul Islam and Secretary General Sibgatullah voiced this concern in a joint statement issued today, 16 November (Monday).

In the statement, the leaders noted: "According to reports published by various international and local media outlets, the proportion of Muslims among those excluded from India's nationwide electoral roll revision process is disproportionately high. In West Bengal alone, approximately 2.7 million voters have been excluded following the adjudication process under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), nearly 70 per cent of whom are Muslims. Despite possessing valid identity documents and family records, many Bengali-speaking Muslims have had their names removed from the electoral rolls. There have also been allegations that, in the course of this process, many of them are being detained on accusations of being 'illegal infiltrators' and forcibly expelled into Bangladesh. Such actions constitute clear violations of international human rights conventions."

Referring to India's existing electoral and constitutional framework, the leaders emphasised: "Under Section 21(3) of India's Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission of India (ECI) is empowered to direct a special revision of electoral rolls. However, Section 22 of the same Act and Rule 21A of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, require proper verification of information, a reasonable opportunity for the individuals concerned to present their cases, and decisions in accordance with established legal procedures before any name is removed from the electoral rolls. Furthermore, Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India guarantee equality before the law and prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, respectively. Therefore, curtailing any citizen's voting rights or subjecting them to discriminatory treatment on the basis of religious identity runs contrary to the constitutional principles of the country."

The statement also highlighted the broader pattern of discrimination against Muslims in India, with the leaders observing: "The process of restricting the civil and fundamental rights of Muslims in India is not an isolated incident; rather, it is part of a long-term state and legal agenda. The controversial Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the National Register of Citizens (NRC) have facilitated the development of a discriminatory framework for determining citizenship on the basis of religious identity. In addition, measures and actions such as the abrogation of Article 370, the law on triple talaq, attempts to impose a Uniform Civil Code (UCC), the Waqf property amendment law, restrictions imposed by various states on cow slaughter and beef consumption, the demolition of mosques, and the demolition of Muslim homes and other structures using bulldozers have undermined the religious, social, and economic rights of Muslims. The current electoral roll revision process is a clear manifestation of this continuing pattern of discriminatory measures, reflecting a policy of 'identify, exclude and expel.'"

Emphasising the fundamental responsibility of the state to protect the rights of its citizens, the leaders declared: "Ensuring citizens' voting rights and security is one of the primary responsibilities of any state. Depriving any community of its voting rights or subjecting its members to harassment over questions of citizenship on the basis of their religious identity is wholly unacceptable.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

Text of My Keynote Address
Delivered at the National Press Day, 2026 celebrations organised by the National Union of Journalists (India), Hyderabad, on 16 November 2026.

*****

Distinguished office-bearers of the National Union of Journalists (India), members of the journalist fraternity, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen.

My greetings to all of you on #NationalPressDay2026.

I am delighted to address an issue that goes beyond the interests of journalists and media organisations. It concerns the survival of truth, the accountability of power and the foundations of democracy.

Artificial Intelligence is transforming how information is created and disseminated—and how people perceive reality. It offers extraordinary possibilities but also unprecedented dangers. In an age when reality itself can be manufactured, who will defend the truth?

For journalism, this is not merely a technological challenge. It is a test of credibility, independence and courage.

I would like to examine this challenge from a democratic and constitutional perspective.

1. AI AND THE MANUFACTURE OF REALITY

Every major technological revolution has transformed communication. The printing press expanded the dissemination of knowledge; radio and television transformed mass communication; the internet removed geographical barriers. Artificial Intelligence takes this transformation to an entirely different level.

Today, videos, voices, photographs, documents and entire narratives can be fabricated and presented as authentic. The consequences can be devastating: elections manipulated, reputations destroyed, social unrest provoked, national security threatened and the administration of justice compromised.

Yet AI can also assist journalism by analysing vast volumes of information, identifying patterns, translating Indian languages and helping uncover facts.
But one distinction is fundamental: the ability to manufacture information is not the ability to establish truth.

A convincing video is not necessarily genuine evidence. An algorithmically identified pattern is not proof of wrongdoing. A machine can generate a narrative, but it cannot assume responsibility for its veracity.

Verification, corroboration and independent human judgment remain indispensable.

AI may transform the tools of journalism. It must never be allowed to manufacture the truth that journalism is duty-bound to discover.

2. THE PRESS AND DEMOCRACY

A functioning democracy rests on four great institutions: the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary and the Free Press. The first three are constitutional organs of the State. The Press has evolved as the Fourth Estate, performing an equally indispensable democratic function.

Our National Emblem offers an interesting metaphor. The Lion Capital of Ashoka depicts four lions standing back to back. Three are visible; the fourth remains invisible. One could metaphorically associate that invisible fourth lion with the Press—not as a constitutional interpretation, but as a reminder of its indispensable democratic role.

The Legislature makes laws, the Executive implements them and the Judiciary interprets them and safeguards the rule of law. The Press informs citizens, scrutinises power, exposes wrongdoing and gives voice to public concerns.

It is the bridge between governance and the people, telling citizens what is done in their name, with their mandate and, most importantly, with their money.

Article 19(1)(a) of our Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression. The Supreme Court has recognised freedom of the Press as integral to this right, subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

Press freedom is not merely a professional privilege. It is also the citizen's right to receive information and form independent opinions.

The Press is not merely an observer of democracy. It enables citizens to question power and hold those who govern them accountable.

3. MEDIA INDEPENDENCE: FROM WHOM AND WHAT?

We frequently discuss press freedom in terms of censorship, governmental interference and intimidation. But the question of independence goes much deeper.

Independence from whom? Independence from what?

Is the Press independent of governments, political parties, corporate owners, commercial interests, ideological and religious influences? Is it independent of its own prejudices?

A Press free from governmental censorship but controlled by political patrons, corporate owners or ideological loyalties is not truly independent.

First: Independence from political ownership and control.

Political parties, politicians and their associates own, control or influence media organisations. At the same time, business interests increasingly enter politics, while politicians acquire commercial interests.
When business becomes politics and politics becomes business, the media becomes an instrument through which both protect their power and interests.

The expression Godi Media has become a widely used pejorative description of sections of the Indian mainstream media since 2014. It reflects the criticism that sections of the media have been manipulated, subdued or co-opted into functioning as publicity and propaganda instruments for the RSS-BJP political establishment and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The problem is not merely favourable coverage. It is the abandonment of scrutiny: governments are praised, opponents vilified and inconvenient questions suppressed.

As the saying goes, “A dog with a bone in its mouth cannot bark.”

Second: Independence from corporate and commercial interests.

Concentration of media ownership, dependence on advertising and commercial pressures can determine editorial priorities. The same business interests may have stakes in media, access to public finance and influence over political decisions.

Between FY2015 and FY2024, scheduled commercial banks wrote off approximately ₹16.35 lakh crore in bad loans, of which around ₹10 lakh crore was linked to big business houses.

Yet, where is the sustained media scrutiny? Where are the investigations into the beneficiaries and the accountability of those responsible?

When the powerful can influence both the flow of public money and the flow of public information, accountability itself is compromised.

Third: Independence of Journalists from Financial Vulnerability.

Journalists must receive fair and assured remuneration and reasonable employment security. Inadequate wages and precarious employment expose them to inducements and pressures that compromise their professional independence. Fair remuneration and employment security are therefore essential safeguards of independent journalism.

Fair remuneration is not merely an employment obligation; it is an essential safeguard of independent journalism.

Fourth: Independence from ideological and religious influence.

Journalists are entitled to personal political, ideological and religious convictions. But personal beliefs must never become professional prejudices. Ideology must not determine which facts are reported, which victims deserve sympathy or which perpetrators are spared scrutiny.

A journalist who applies different standards according to political allegiance or religious identity is practising partisanship, not independent journalism.

The most dangerous form of media control is not always censorship of what is published. It is control over what is never allowed to become a subject of public scrutiny.

Press independence must therefore be both institutional and intellectual: freedom from external control and freedom from prejudices that compromise professional judgment.

4. SELECTIVE JOURNALISM

Media capture by political, corporate and ideological interests has a direct consequence: selective journalism. Some events are amplified, others buried; some victims command national outrage, while others disappear from public consciousness.
Let me cite five examples.

First: Naxalism and Maoist insurgency.

For decades, sections of the intellectual and media establishment romanticised Naxalite and Maoist insurgents as revolutionaries and champions of the oppressed.

Marginalised populations have suffered genuine injustice, exploitation and deprivation. Their grievances deserve redressal. But reporting those grievances is fundamentally different from romanticising armed groups that exploit them to advance a violent, anti-democratic ideology.

Did the media adequately expose how deprivation and alienation were exploited to recruit cadres and perpetuate violence?

When journalism romanticises violent ideologies and neglects their victims, it risks becoming a propaganda instrument and force-multiplier for the very forces it ought to expose.

Second: The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus.

The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus from their ancestral homeland remain one of the darkest and most shameful chapters in democratic India's history. Hindus were subjected to targeted killings, terror, threats and religious persecution. An entire Hindu community was driven out of Kashmir, and the Indian State was complicit.

And what did the Indian media do? Where was its outrage? Where were its investigations and sustained campaigns for justice and the safe return of the displaced?

The media's failure was not simply inadequate coverage. It was a complicit silence in the face of the genocide and religious cleansing of an entire community.

By its silence, the media helped erase the suffering of Kashmiri Hindus from the national conscience. That is an indictment of the media as much as it is of the State.

Third: The religious persecution of Hindus in the Northeast.

In the Christian-majority states of Mizoram and Meghalaya, Hindus have been facing severe religious persecution and discrimination. In some instances, they have been denied even the basic right to perform the last rites of their dead, to cremate their own family members in accordance with their religious traditions.

What could be more fundamental than this right? And where is the national media? Where are the headlines, investigations and expressions of outrage?

When the media turns a blind eye to the persecution of a community, it abandons the victims and shields the perpetrators from scrutiny.

Fourth: Double standards in reporting religiously sensitive crimes.

There is a glaring asymmetry in crime reporting. When the victim is Christian or Muslim, or the accused is Hindu, religious identity is often prominently highlighted. But when Hindus are victims, or the accused is Christian or Muslim, that identity disappears into generic descriptions or silence.

Why should the same journalistic standards not apply to everyone?

I demand equal seriousness of investigation, prominence of coverage and accountability, irrespective of the community involved.

The test of secular journalism is not whether it ignores religion, but whether it applies the same standards of fairness and scrutiny to everyone.

Fifth: Neutrality Must Not Become Complicity.

The media cannot be neutral between the perpetrator and the victim. Silence in the face of oppression emboldens the perpetrator and abandons the victim. Neutrality that fails to distinguish between the two is not impartiality; it is complicity.

Journalistic independence demands an unwavering commitment to truth and equal scrutiny of every government, political party, ideology and institution, irrespective of whose interests are affected.

5. FREEDOM AFTER SPEECH

A remark attributed to Idi Amin, the former President of Uganda, captures a fundamental danger: “There is freedom of speech, but I cannot guarantee freedom after speech.”

It exposes the hollowness of a freedom that exists only so long as it does not inconvenience those in power.

This brings me to an important constitutional proposition.

Article 19(1)(a), while guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression, is not adequate by itself to provide the explicit institutional recognition and safeguards that an independent Press requires. The Constitution must recognise the Free Press as an independent Fourth Estate of our democracy.

As National President of the Sarvjan Sanatan Party @sarvjansp, I affirm our commitment to pursuing a constitutional amendment to provide explicit constitutional recognition and status to the Press, so that not only freedom of speech but, importantly, freedom after speech is constitutionally guaranteed and enforced.

If the Press is indispensable to democracy, why should its institutional independence and constitutional status remain without explicit constitutional recognition?

I leave this question before this distinguished gathering.

Thank you.

Privacy vs Press Freedom: Where Should the Line Be Drawn?

Introduction

🌟 The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, has reignited the constitutional debate between individual privacy and freedom of the press. The challenge is to protect personal dignity without undermining investigative journalism and the public's right to know.

Main Body

🌟 Constitutional Balance: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of expression, while Article 21 protects the right to privacy, recognised in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

🌟 Journalistic Independence: Mandatory consent for personal information could restrict investigative reporting and discourage whistleblowers from exposing wrongdoing.

🌟 Public Interest Test: In R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (1994), the Supreme Court distinguished legitimate public reporting from unjustified intrusion into private life.

🌟 Sting Operations: R.K. Anand v. Registrar, Delhi High Court (2009) recognised their public value in exposing misconduct, while Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014) cautioned against treating sting operations as immunity from criminal liability.

🌟 Media Accountability: Sahara v. SEBI (2012) recognised temporary postponement of publication where publicity threatens a fair trial.

🌟 International Practice: The US, UK, Brazil and Kenya provide different forms of journalistic exemptions within data-protection frameworks.

Challenges

🌟 Balancing privacy with transparency and accountability.

🌟 Protecting confidential sources and whistleblowers.

🌟 Preventing trial by media and reputational damage.

🌟 Avoiding misuse of privacy laws to suppress scrutiny.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Excessive consent requirements may create indirect censorship.

🌟 Unclear exemptions can generate regulatory uncertainty.

🌟 Investigative journalism may become vulnerable to legal intimidation.

🌟 Unrestricted reporting can violate individual dignity and fair-trial rights.

Way Forward

🌟 Introduce a clearly defined public-interest exemption.

🌟 Establish independent and proportionate oversight.

🌟 Protect confidential journalistic sources.

🌟 Develop safeguards against trial by media.

🌟 Harmonise data protection with constitutional freedoms.

Highlighted Keywords

🌟 Constitutional Balancing: Reconciling competing fundamental rights without allowing either to become absolute.

🌟 Public Interest: Information necessary for democratic accountability, not merely public curiosity.

🌟 Prior Restraint: Government-imposed restriction on publication before it occurs.

🌟 Trial by Media: Media coverage that prejudges guilt before judicial determination.

🌟 Proportionality: Restricting a right only to the extent necessary for a legitimate objective.

Conclusion

🌟 A mature democracy must protect both the individual's right to dignity and the press's duty to question power. Privacy must not become a shield for misconduct, nor press freedom a licence for intrusion.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

LALIT MODI ISSUES STATEMENT ON BRITISH CITIZENSHIP AND INACCURATE MEDIA REPORTING

Founder of the Indian Premier League challenges misleading accounts of his departure from India, cites judicial findings and warns of legal action against defamatory reporting.

LONDON | 16 NOVEMBER 2026

Lalit Modi, Founder of the Indian Premier League (IPL), has issued the following statement in response to recent media coverage concerning his British citizenship and historical legal matters.

STATEMENT BY LALIT MODI

“A section of the Indian media has portrayed my acquisition of British citizenship as the development of someone who fled allegations and whom India is now attempting to ‘bring back’.

The entire premise of such reporting is false. I intend to pursue appropriate legal remedies against false and defamatory reports in all jurisdictions available to me.

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF MY DEPARTURE FROM INDIA

I left India in 2010 because of credible threats to my life from the underworld, three days after my armed police protection was withdrawn without notice.

At the time of my departure, no FIR existed against me.

In a letter to the Enforcement Directorate, the Additional Commissioner of the Mumbai Police confirmed that my security protection had been provided on the basis of intelligence received from central agencies concerning threats to my life.

When my Indian passport was subsequently cancelled at the instance of the Enforcement Directorate, the Delhi High Court examined the circumstances, set aside the revocation in 2014 and restored my passport.

NO CHARGESHEET OR CRIMINAL PROSECUTION

In more than sixteen years, no chargesheet has ever been filed against me in any court in India. No criminal prosecution concerning these matters has been launched against me in any Indian court.

An FIR was registered in Chennai in October 2010 following a complaint by N. Srinivasan, then Secretary of the BCCI. I maintain that the complaint was an act of vendetta intended to remove me from the IPL, following my opposition to Mr Srinivasan’s conflict of interest arising from his simultaneous positions as a BCCI office-bearer, member of the IPL Governing Council and owner of Chennai Super Kings.

In January 2015, the Supreme Court held that Mr Srinivasan suffered from a conflict of interest and was disqualified from holding office in the BCCI.

The Chennai Police itself prepared a closure report in February 2015, finding that the contracts in question were commercial in nature and disclosed no crime.

The Bombay High Court has twice found that the allegations of fraud concerning the IPL media-rights contract, which formed the basis of the FIR lodged by N. Srinivasan, were not made out.

There is no money-laundering complaint or prosecution against me. A complaint under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act depends upon a predicate offence, which, in the matters alleged against me, does not exist.

Interpol has confirmed in writing that it holds no records of criminal diffusions or alert notices against me.

REGULATORY AND JUDICIAL FINDINGS

Every regulatory proceeding that has been decided so far has ended in my favour.

The personal penalty imposed upon me in connection with the second season of the IPL, conducted in South Africa in 2009, was completely set aside by the Appellate Tribunal.

Every time an independent authority has examined the actions taken against me, it has found in my favour.

MY LEGAL POSITION

Extradition is a legal process concerning persons facing criminal proceedings or convicted of offences. I am neither.

There is no chargesheet, no criminal charge, no prosecution and no Interpol Red Notice against me.

MY BRITISH CITIZENSHIP

The United Kingdom has been my home since 2010.

British authorities granted me leave to remain many years ago after examining my circumstances in full.

I subsequently applied for British citizenship, completed the established legal process and received approval from the Home Office in July 2026.

I have never sought immunity of any kind, nor do I need it.

I am proud of my British citizenship and grateful to the United Kingdom, which has been my home for more than sixteen years.

NOTICE REGARDING FALSE AND DEFAMATORY REPORTING

I have always respected the freedom of the press and recognise the right of journalists to report fairly and accurately on matters of public interest.

However, that freedom does not justify the deliberate publication or republication of false allegations, the distortion of established facts or the misrepresentation of judicial findings.

I hereby put publishers, editors, journalists, broadcasters and digital media platforms on notice that I will pursue the strongest appropriate legal action, including proceedings for libel and defamation, against persons responsible for deliberate and defamatory misreporting contrary to established facts and judicial records.

Where appropriate, I will seek corrections, retractions, damages and all other remedies available under applicable law.

I will not allow the repeated publication of demonstrably false allegations to go unchallenged.

My record must be judged by the facts, the evidence and the decisions of the courts — not by the repetition of allegations.”

LALIT MODI
Founder, Indian Premier League

I think I am the first AmEx customer, going back to 2008. 

(Okay, I am sure there are more, I am just bragging). But 2008 is quite some time now.

I have been a very early adopter / user of digital money, much much before Paytm happened. When Paytm happened (I was there, three times), I stopped carrying my Wallet/cash. It was futile . . .  

In all these decades of AmEx usage, I have primarily oscillated between a Platinum Reserve and a Platinum Charge card. I always wanted the Black card, which did not happen, at least till now. Sigh!

There is literally no event in my memory where I would have paid more to use an AmEx card or where a card would have been declined. Needless to say I always had a Visa or a MC and I would be mindful enough to use an appropriate network at appropriate places. 

I have never ever gamed the card and or any programmes that AmEx ran, never referred anyone either. I think the only things that I would have used is the 10X or 5X programmes which were quite straight forward.

In all these years, decades, I have had different relationship managers assigned but I have always preferred to go to the chat option within the app and get an answer to my query. The chat option, at least for me has been very robust till date.

I don't recollect having taken and screen recording and or screen shot of my conversations with AmEx because the level of trust was, to my mind, unbreachable.

I have had replacement cards delivered to me in 24 hours, within/outside India, unauthorised charges worth  hundreds of pounds reversed, no questions asked etc etc.

There was this relationship where, I would care less about points redemptions, their value etc because the sheer peace of mind that this relationship brought to the table was priceless. So much so, I had not received (probably missed by me), annual renewal benefits for my Platinum Charge Card for last cycle . . . it is not that I did not want them, it's just that, I was perhaps so sure that I can have them whenever I want . . .

With the current fiasco, when a million of my points were arbitrarily taken away, I was confused in my mind - AmEx has one of the best technology stacks out there in the industry, perhaps the best and I had this relationship that was flawless. I could not put a finger on this decision - was it a tech issue or was it a deliberate policy decision.

Given the emails and replies that I see on X (I had not reached out to AmEx on chat and neither did I receive any comms till date from them. I did email them after they asked me to based on my earlier post on X), I see this was a deliberate action, a policy decision they have now reversed. I reached out to AmEx today on chat and they confirmed it as well. Needless to say they are sorry and are reversing the arbitrary takedown of points. (see chat attached)

Even when I get back my million points, I don't think this trust deficit can be rebuild very easily. Or maybe they don't want it to be rebuilt either, which is possible.

And honestly, I am not trying to be mean here, who ever decided this move, should literally be hauled up for such a brazen decision. Not only that it is a very classic case for the regulator to actually come in a read the riot act - both for card companies and for consumers who misuse. 

There should be clear do's and don's. India is a large enough market for the regulator to give directions. Devaluing points, arbitrarily or sneakily taking away points, consumers getting away by gaming the system el at should all be put to rest.

I feel sad for the break of trust in this relationship with @AmexIndia @AmericanExpress

Illegal Infiltration & Fake Documentation:-A Real Case I Handled

Home Minister @AmitShah ji has held that the population of Muslims in India has increased due to illegal infiltration. Let me share a real case I personally handled about 5–6 years ago in Mumbai, one among many that reveal how deep this problem runs. Please do read to understand the rot.

1. The Client’s Request:- One evening after court hours, a Muslim gentleman known to me came to my office. He had given his premises in Govandi, Mumbai, on a leave and license agreement to a family of 6/7 people.
Even after the agreement expired, the family refused to vacate.

I perused his papers and assured him of appropriate legal action. He then asked if the matter could be resolved sooner than usual.
When I explained that such cases typically take little time, he hesitated and what he said next stunned me.

2. The Shocking Revelation :- He quietly said, “Sir, those tenants are not Indians, they are Bangladeshis.”

That single sentence changed everything. Two thoughts struck me instantly:
1. Why hadn’t he mentioned this earlier?
2. How did they even get valid Aadhaar and PAN cards as visible in the agreement?

3. The Investigation:- On examining the documents, everything looked perfectly legitimate; Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, even voter ID.
We filed RTIs, involved the local police, and began to dig deeper.

Gradually, the truth surfaced, the birth certificate forming the basis of all these documents was forged.

Using that single forged certificate from 1967, the accused had created a full legal identity for himself and his family, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, and voter ID.

4. A Web of Fraud:- It didn’t stop there. The man had used the same method to obtain documents for his wife and children. His son was even married to an Indian Muslim woman, effectively merging into the Indian population.

During the investigation, we uncovered an organized network, a full-fledged industry operating to regularize illegal immigrants by manufacturing fake Indian identities that pass every verification test.

5. The Larger Problem:-India’s diversity makes such infiltration even easier. People entering from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, or Nepal often resemble locals making visual identification almost impossible.

Add to this the corruption that exists from border checkpoints to administrative offices, and you have a perfect ecosystem for illegal population growth.

In this very case, we found the involvement of certain officials, and shockingly, even a few lawyers.

6. A Moment That Exposed the Rot:- One of those lawyers, representing the Bangladeshi accused, told my Muslim junior,
“How can you do this? This is a matter of religion.”
My junior stood firm and warned him of a complaint before the Bar Council.

This single moment revealed how some individuals, blinded by religious or political motives, are actively protecting those who illegally enter and settle in India.

7. The Unanswered Question:- 
This wasn’t the only case, I have come across several similar ones.
Despite being aware of this menace for years, successive governments have failed to implement a robust national mechanism to identify and deport such individuals.

8. The Hope:- Now that the Home Minister himself has spoken openly about the issue, one can only hope it translates into real, concrete action. India needs a firm, technology-backed, corruption-proof mechanism to detect and remove non-Indians living here on forged documents.

Illegal infiltration is not just a demographic concern, it’s a threat to national integrity, law, and fairness. The time for acknowledgment is over.
The time for action has arrived.

🚨PLYMOUTH, MA - Today I was assaulted and robbed by John Nagle, #030 Assistant Chief Court Officer of Plymouth and Barnstable Courts. 

I went into Plymouth Courthouse to be present for support for a friend who was filing litigation pro se on his case. He is an alienated parent whose life has been depleted and destroyed by his wife (in big part due to coercive advice from her legal counsel). 

While my friend was speaking with the person behind the counter, I pulled out my phone and started recording, to document the unacceptable response/tone in which this public employee was speaking to my friend. 

The court officer aggressively approached me, asked if I was recording, and immediately snatched my phone out of my hand. He told me I have to delete the video or I’m not getting my phone back. I refused to delete the video and he grabbed me and started pushing me out of the courthouse, while still refusing to give me back my phone. 

The back & forth continued outside. I asked for him to provide me the MGL or SJC ruling that gives him authority to confiscate my phone because I won’t delete the video. He showed me nothing but the poster on the wall that says recording is prohibited, to which I argued that a policy posted on the wall doesn’t give him explicit authority to demand I delete the video or he keeps my phone. 

So I called the police and reported being assaulted and robbed by the court officer. 

The police came & they all started talking in circles. I asked them to bring out the court magistrate. Court magistrate came outside and told me if I didn’t delete the video I would be charged with wiretapping and/or intimidation of a witness and/or obstruction/interruption of a court proceeding - to which I reminded her that I wasn’t in a court room and I wasn’t recording a court proceeding. She replied “details don’t matter - you have to delete the video or you’re going to be charged with a felony”. 

I told them to charge me and gave the police officer my ID. 

The police went inside with the magistrate and court officer and about 5 minutes later they made the court officer come out and return my phone. 

Did I violate the courthouse policy? Sure. 
Does that give the court officer the right or authority to steal my phone and physically remove me from the courthouse when I showed zero signs of aggression and/or refusal to leave? Absolutely NOT. 

The proper response would have been to tell me I couldn’t record and ask me to exit the courthouse if I refused to comply. THEN the court officer should call the police to escort me out. But I didn’t refuse to comply because I had no chance to say or do anything before he stole my phone and started dragging me out. This court officer was on a power trip, used excessive force, and completely ESCALATED a situation that could’ve been prevented without wasting everyone’s time & police resources. And this man gets paid upwards of $110,000 a year. Unacceptable. 

And this is the exact reason we need to fight to remove these camera-in-court policies. When we are mistreated by a public employee in a courthouse, how else are we supposed to document it?

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
“Wouldn’t have happened if all were driverless Waymo cars.” Prove it. You cannot establish what would have happened in an imaginary crash involving four different vehicles running different software. Declaring your favorite brand incapable of the same outcome is advertising dressed up as analysis.

Waymo has its own documented record of dangerous failures. In 2024, it recalled software covering 444 vehicles after two Waymos struck the same towed pickup truck. Another recall covered 672 vehicles because the system could fail to avoid poles and similar objects. In 2025, a recall covered 1,212 vehicles over collisions with chains, gates, and similar barriers. These were safety defects, not complaints about whether passengers liked the seats.

Then came the school buses. A December 2025 recall covered 3,067 vehicles because Waymos could stop for a school bus, then start moving again before its flashing red lights or extended stop arm had been withdrawn. On November 6, 2026, federal regulators opened an investigation into whether that fix worked: most of the reported incidents identified in their earlier investigation occurred after the stated repair date.

The National Transportation Safety Board documented a January 12, 2026 incident in Austin in which a Waymo stopped for a school bus, asked remote assistance whether its signals were active, received an incorrect “No,” and drove past while the stop arms remained extended. The bus was loading students. No crash occurred, but passing a school bus during boarding creates an obvious danger. Removing the driver did not remove human error; a remote worker’s wrong answer helped send the vehicle forward.

The reports I posted also show a Waymo entering an active police scene, another blocking an on-duty fire truck during a standoff, and residents describing roughly 50 driverless Waymos coming through an Atlanta neighborhood. Police officers, firefighters, children boarding buses, and residents are real people using public streets. They do not exist to accommodate a company’s software failures.

And there are so many more examples. Face it. You're parasocially attached to a robocar and you're making crap up to defend it.

Meanwhile, America made enormous road-safety gains long before commercial robotaxis. U.S. road deaths fell from 51,091 in 1980 to an estimated 36,640 in 2025, about 28% fewer deaths. The death rate fell from 3.35 per 100 million miles in 1980 to an estimated 1.02 in the first half of 2026, about 70% lower. Those figures do not make every road safe. They demolish the claim that progress requires Waymo.

America does not need Waymo. Safer vehicles, seat belts, road design, traffic enforcement, and public transportation do not require giving this particular company permission to operate. Treating every human-caused crash as a Waymo advertisement while brushing aside Waymo’s own dangerous failures is corporate fandom, not serious concern for public safety.

And even when a Waymo operates exactly as intended, it still cannot carry people who must remain seated in their complex power wheelchairs. Defenders keep promoting a service that excludes us while threatening the income that keeps existing accessible taxis operating. Your preferred robotaxi is no excuse to sacrifice our transportation or our civil rights.

(Sources: NHTSA recall records and November 2026 investigation notice, National Transportation Safety Board, Federal Highway Administration, Associated Press, NBC News, and the local reports shown above.)
